recipe.history:
Kimchi is one of the oldest and most deeply rooted fermented foods in Korean culinary history, with documented origins stretching back over two thousand years to the Three Kingdoms period of the Korean peninsula. Early versions of kimchi were simple salted vegetables preserved against the brutal winters, but the transformation into the spiced, fermented napa cabbage dish the world knows today came after the Columbian Exchange introduced chili peppers to Korea in the late 16th century. The addition of gochugaru — coarsely ground Korean red pepper — fundamentally changed the flavor profile, giving kimchi its characteristic heat and brilliant crimson color. Fermented in large ceramic onggi pots buried in the earth to maintain steady temperatures, kimchi became a year-round staple of Korean life, a symbol of communal labor, preservation wisdom, and the deep Korean understanding that time and bacteria are the most important ingredients of all.

Kimchi made its way into American culinary consciousness gradually, first through the large Korean-American communities of Los Angeles and New York, then explosively through the Korean taco and Korean BBQ movements of the 2000s and 2010s. Food trucks like Kogi BBQ in Los Angeles demonstrated that fermented, funky, fiery Korean flavors could be married to familiar American formats — the taco, the burrito, and inevitably, the burger. Kimchi's natural acidity and crunch made it a revelation as a burger topping, cutting through fat the way pickles do but with far more complexity. Chefs began pressing kimchi directly into beef patties, letting its fermented tang permeate the meat and its heat meld with the caramelized crust of a hard sear. The result was a burger that tasted like it had been fermenting in flavor for generations.

I remember the first time I put kimchi in a burger patty — it was a cold Tuesday in November and I had a half-jar of aged kimchi in the fridge that had been quietly working for three weeks. I chopped it fine, squeezed out the brine, and folded it directly into the ground beef with a little sesame oil. When it hit the cast iron, the smell was unlike anything I had cooked before — the sour, spicy, almost barnyard funk of the kimchi mingling with rendered beef fat and toasted sesame. My partner came into the kitchen with the look of someone who was not sure if dinner was going to be a success or a story we tell later. It was a success. We stood at the counter and ate them before we even thought about sitting down.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef burger patty, and that is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a preference — it is the temperature at which beef fat renders into something silky and luxurious rather than waxy and greasy, the temperature at which the muscle fibers relax just enough to stay tender while still carrying a deep, mineral, beefy flavor. Cooking beyond this point drives out moisture irreversibly, collapses the fat pockets, and produces a dense, gray, joyless disk that tastes of obligation rather than pleasure. The pink center of a medium rare burger is not a safety compromise — it is the entire point. Season, sear, rest, and trust the thermometer. Everything else is theater.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
120g well-fermented napa cabbage kimchi, finely chopped and squeezed dry
neutral oil for cooking (grapeseed or canola)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Mix with the dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the sides of the bowl.
2. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled in size.

3. Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Shape each into a smooth ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced 3 inches apart.
4. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof for 45 minutes until puffy. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
5. Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack to cool completely before slicing.
6. Make the gochujang mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, gochujang, rice vinegar, honey, and garlic powder in a small bowl until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Make the kimchi slaw: Combine the chopped kimchi, shredded green cabbage, mayonnaise, rice vinegar, sesame oil, sesame seeds, and sugar in a medium bowl. Toss well and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

8. Make the kimchi patties: Place chopped, squeezed-dry kimchi in a large bowl with the ground beef, sesame oil, gochugaru, soy sauce, salt, and black pepper. Mix gently with your hands until just combined — do not overwork the meat. Divide into 4 equal portions and shape into patties roughly 3/4 inch thick, slightly wider than the buns to account for shrinkage. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet or grill pan over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep crust.

10. Flip patties once and cook for an additional 2 to 3 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Remove patties from heat when they register 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) at the thickest point for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest for 3 to 4 minutes — the temperature will rise slightly during resting.
11. While the patties rest, slice the buns in half and toast cut-side down in the residual fat in the skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

12. Assemble: Spread gochujang mayo generously on both the top and bottom bun. Place a leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun. Set the patty on the lettuce. Pile a generous mound of kimchi slaw on top of the patty. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
